big_idea: In a growing pattern, each term gets bigger by the same amount; in a shrinking pattern, each term gets smaller by the same amount.
learning_intention: We are learning to build growing and shrinking patterns and to write the rule using +N or -N notation.
student_learning_goal: I can build a growing parade and a shrinking parade and tell my partner the rule for each.
success_criteria: I can build a growing parade where each term gets bigger by the same amount.
I can build a shrinking parade where each term gets smaller by the same amount.
I can write the rule using +N (for growing) or -N (for shrinking) notation.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from Lesson 1 (REPEATING, GROWING, SHRINKING already on)

Pre-built example parades for the +N / -N reveal: (1) growing +2 (2 Beas, 4 Beas, 6 Beas, 8 Beas), (2) growing +1 (1 Finn, 2 Finns, 3 Finns, 4 Finns), (3) shrinking -3 (10 Beas, 7 Beas, 4 Beas, 1 Bea — for advanced groups)
Sticky notes pre-prepared with rule labels (+1, +2, +3, +5, -1, -2, -3) and blanks for invented rules
Class formative tracker for Lesson 2 (provided in assessment_suite stage)
Optional: small whiteboards or scrap paper for pairs to write +N rules

minds_on.hook: Yesterday we said 'getting bigger' and 'one more.' Today we give the rule a NAME using a + or a - and a number.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Lay parade 1 (growing +2: 2 Beas, 4 Beas, 6 Beas, 8 Beas across 4 cells). Hold up Coco.

Say to students: 'Friends, look at this growing parade. Read it with me: 2 Beas, 4 Beas, 6 Beas, 8 Beas. From term 1 to term 2, how many MORE Beas do we add?' (2 more.) 'From term 2 to term 3?' (2 more.) 'From term 3 to term 4?' (2 more.) 'Same amount every time! Mathematicians call this a +2 rule. We write it like this.' Write +2 on a sticky and place it next to the parade. 'Plus two means: each term is the term before, plus two more.'

Lay parade 2 (growing +1: 1 Finn, 2 Finns, 3 Finns, 4 Finns). Read together. Ask: 'What is the rule? +____?' (+1.) Place a +1 sticky.

Now lay a shrinking parade (5 Beas, 4 Beas, 3 Beas, 2 Beas). Read. Ask: 'What is happening?' (subtract one each time.) 'So the rule is MINUS one. We write -1.' Place a -1 sticky. 'Today YOU build growing and shrinking parades AND name the rule.'
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the example parades.
Read each parade aloud and count the change between terms.
Help name each rule using +N or -N notation.
Repeat the rule notations aloud as a class ('+2 means add two each time').

action.activity_name: Build the Rule, Loop the Step

steps.instruction: Whole group demo: build a growing +3 parade slowly with the class (3 Beas, 6 Beas, 9 Beas, 12 Beas). After each term, take a Core Loop Frame (M5) and place it across the GAP between two terms — explain that the loop now marks the JUMP, not the core. The loop highlights the constant change of +3 between each pair of terms.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Watch this loop. It's not circling the core today — there is no core in a growing pattern. The loop is showing the JUMP between terms. From 3 Beas to 6 Beas, the jump is +3. From 6 to 9, the jump is +3. Same jump every time. THAT is the rule.'

steps.instruction: Partner build round 1: each pair gets Animal Cards (M1), one Parade Strip (M2), one Core Loop Frame (M5), and a stack of sticky notes. Their job: build TWO growing parades — one with a +1 rule, one with a +2 rule. Loop one jump in each. Write the rule on a sticky.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two growing parades. First a +1, then a +2. Loop the jump on each. Write the rule on a sticky beside it. When you are done, find another pair and try to read THEIR rule before they tell you.'

steps.instruction: Partner build round 2: now build TWO shrinking parades — one with a -1 rule, one with a -2 rule. Same loop-and-sticky routine. The challenge: a shrinking parade ends when there are zero animals — pairs must decide where to start so their parade has at least 4 terms.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now switch — shrinking. -1 first, then -2. Plan ahead: for -2 to make 4 terms, you have to start with at least 8 animals. Math pre-planning! Loop the jump, write the rule, swap parades with a different pair.'

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge for fast pairs: invent a rule the teacher has not shown yet (e.g., +5, -3, +10, +0 special case). Build it. Trade with another pair and have them name it.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to extending pairs: 'Trade your rule sticky with another pair. Now you have a NEW rule. Build the parade — but only the FIRST 3 terms. Then ask the other pair to predict TERM 4 without showing them.'

steps.instruction: Circulate. Use the Lesson 2 formative tracker. Look especially for: did the child use the +N / -N notation in writing AND speech? Could they invent a rule and apply it consistently? Did they self-correct when their growing pattern accidentally doubled (×2 instead of +2)?
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask one child: 'What is the rule of your parade?' Then: 'How do you KNOW it is +2 and not ×2?' (The child should say: 'because we add 2 each time, not double.') Record on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay with +1 and -1 rules using small numbers (1–5 Beas per term). Provide pre-written sticky notes (+1 and -1) so writing is not a barrier. Pair with a confident peer.
differentiation.for_extending: Use +3, +5, -2, -3 rules with larger numbers per term (up to 12 animals per cell — pairs may need 2 sets of M1). Stretch question: 'If your +3 parade kept going, what would term 10 be? Tell me without building it.'
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use a sentence frame: 'My rule is +___. From term 1 to term 2 I added ___.' Allow the child to point to the rule sticky while saying the number. Provide pre-printed +N stickies (+1 to +5) so writing is not the barrier.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After building, the pair stands up and acts out the growing pattern by adding one more body movement at each step (e.g., term 1 = 1 clap, term 2 = 2 claps, term 3 = 3 claps). For shrinking, start big and remove one each time.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child build a growing pattern with a constant +N change? Can they build a shrinking pattern with a constant -N change? Do they write the rule in +N / -N notation? Can they recognize when a 'growing' pattern is actually multiplying (×2) versus adding (+2)?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the appropriate column on the Lesson 2 formative tracker.

discussion_prompts: Who built a growing parade with the BIGGEST jump? What was the rule?
Did anyone build a shrinking parade where the rule made the parade end exactly at zero? How did you plan for that?
Yesterday we sorted patterns into three types. Today we named the rule with +N or -N. Could the SAME parade have two different rules? Why or why not?
consolidation.exit_routine: On the way out the door, each child names one growing rule and one shrinking rule using +N or -N notation ('My growing rule is +___. My shrinking rule is -___'). Teacher records who can chant rules confidently.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Class formative tracker for C1.1 (growing/shrinking identification) and C1.3 (rule naming with +N/-N notation), plus completed student worksheet 'Name the Jump'.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Naming the rule using +N / -N notation is a Grade 2 leap from Grade 1's letter-rule labels. The teacher needs evidence of who can write and apply the notation before Lesson 3 (table of values) requires reading Term/Value pairs and matching them to a +N rule.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Naming the Rule — from informal language to +N/-N notation
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: L2 elevates yesterday's 'getting bigger' to today's '+N' notation. The cognitive demand is symbolic — children must translate 'each parade has two more animals than the one before' into '+2.' Step 1 (whole-group +3 demo) and Step 4 (invented rule challenge) are the keystones. The walkthrough below covers the move from verbal description to written notation.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Carpet has the +3 demo strip cleared and ready. Each pair has Animal Cards, Parade Strip, Core Loop Frame, and sticky notes. Anchor chart has columns labelled +1, +2, +3, +4, +5, -1, -2, -3, -4 ready to capture invented rules.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
During the whole-group demo: place 3 Beas in cell 1, 6 Beas in cell 2, 9 Beas in cell 3, 12 Beas in cell 4. Now ask: 'How many more Beas does each new term have?' Listen for informal answers ('three more,' 'three each time'). Confirm and translate: 'Yes — each term has three MORE than the one before. We write that as PLUS THREE, with a + sign and the number 3.' Write '+3' on the chart. 'This is the rule.'

Now ask: 'If I show you JUST the +3 rule and nothing else, can someone build a NEW +3 parade with different animals?' Take a volunteer. They build, say, 1 Finn, 4 Finns, 7 Finns, 10 Finns. Pause: that's a +3 rule, but starting from 1 instead of 3. 'Is this still a +3 rule?' YES. The rule says how MUCH each term grows by, not where it starts. Write the second example next to the first on the chart: '+3 starting at 1: 1, 4, 7, 10. +3 starting at 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Same rule, different start.' This is a major G2 conceptual move.

Send children to partner work. Walk to a pair attempting their first +1 build. They build 1 Bea, 2 Beas, 3 Beas, 4 Beas — easy. Now ask: 'Same +1 rule, but start at 5 instead. Build it.' If they build 5, 6, 7, 8 confidently, they own the rule. If they default back to 1, 2, 3, 4 because that's what they just did, they've memorized the build, not the rule.

For Step 4 (shrinking): walk to a pair with a -2 strip that has 6, 4, 2, 0 (correctly ending at zero). Praise it. Now ask: 'What if I gave you a -3 rule starting at 12? Build it.' They should produce 12, 9, 6, 3. If they do, they've fully owned the +N/-N notation. Record on the tracker.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Says 'getting bigger by some' or 'growing by lots' — hasn't translated to +N notation.
(Mid) Names +1 / +2 / -1 / -2 confidently but stalls on +3 or larger. Comfortable with unit-and-binary rules only.
(Strong) Names rule, transfers to new starting term, transfers to different animals.
(Stretched) Invents a rule (e.g., +5 or -3) and applies it consistently across 5+ terms with no help.
common_misconceptions: The rule is tied to the starting number. (Child thinks +3 specifically means 3, 6, 9, 12 and not 1, 4, 7, 10.)
The +N notation is decorative. (Child writes +2 on a sticky but builds an irregular pattern, not connecting the symbol to the build behaviour.)
Shrinking patterns end at the last cell drawn. (Child doesn't see that -2 starting at 6 ends at 0 and can't go below — misses the natural floor.)
recovery_moves: Insist on translating 'how many more' to '+N' explicitly. Don't accept 'three more' — say 'so we write that as PLUS THREE — show me the + sign.' Force the symbol.
Use the same-rule-different-start move. Two strips, both +3, different starting numbers. Make the rule independence visible.
For shrinking: ask 'how far can your -2 rule go before there's nothing left?' Make the floor explicit. This deepens the rule into a real-world constraint.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of C1.1 + C1.3 — building growing and shrinking patterns and naming the rule using +N / -N notation.

parts_outline.task: Show four pre-built parade strips (4 cells each): A (1, 3, 5, 7 Beas — +2), B (10, 8, 6, 4 Beas — -2), C (1, 2, 3, 4 Beas — +1), D (8, 5, 2 — but only 3 cells filled, -3). Beside each, a writing line: 'Rule: ____'. Student writes the rule using +N or -N notation.

Show an empty 4-cell parade strip. Above it: 'Build a growing parade with the rule +3. Start with ___ Beas.' Student picks a starting number and fills all 4 cells with the right number of Beas (or numbers).

Show an empty 4-cell parade strip. Above it: 'Build a shrinking parade. Pick your own rule. Make sure it has at least 4 terms.' Below: 'My rule: -____.' Student picks a rule and a starting number, then fills 4 cells.
